title: HW 19
subtitle: Ch. 8 — Kinetic Molecular Theory, Gas Units & Combined Gas Law

questions.q: Which statements are true about the Kinetic Molecular Theory?
opts: Individual gas molecules may change speeds over time.
Pressure is a result of the collisions of gas particles hitting the sides of the container in which they are housed.
As gas atoms collide, they will slow down over time and eventually stop moving.
Gases obey the kinetic molecular theory best at low temperatures.

The kinetic energy of a sample of gas is proportional to the temperature in Kelvin. This means that gas molecules in a sample that is hot will move faster than gas molecules in a sample that is cooler.
Gases are assumed to not take up any space relative to size of the container.
questions.note: Collisions are elastic, so molecules never slow down and stop. Gases behave most ideally at HIGH temperature and low pressure, not low temperature.

questions.q: Select the gas with the highest average velocity at 298 K.
questions.note: Same temperature = same average kinetic energy. KE = ½mv², so the lightest molecule (H₂, 2.02 g/mol) moves fastest.

questions.q: On the left is a magnified view of a very small portion of liquid water in a closed container. Which magnified view would best represent what it looks like after the water evaporates?
questions.note: Evaporation is a physical change: the H₂O molecules stay intact (one O bonded to two H) and simply spread far apart. Picture 2 shows H₂ and O₂ (the water broke apart), Picture 4 is still packed like a liquid, and the empty circle is not the answer.

questions.q: What would 26.4 ºF be in ºC?
FLASHBACK: Convert 197.1 °F to Celsius. Round your answer to 1 decimal.
Convert 50.77 °C to Kelvin. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.
Convert 49.91 °C to Kelvin. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.
Which statements are true?
opts: As volume increases pressure will decrease.
As you decrease the temperature of a gas, the volume will decrease.
Volume of a gas is directly proportional to pressure at constant temperature and number of moles.
As moles in a container increase, pressure will decrease.
Volume of a gas is directly proportional to temperature in Kelvin at constant pressure and number of moles.
questions.note: Boyle: V and P are INVERSELY proportional. Charles: V and T (K) are directly proportional. More moles in the same container means MORE pressure.

questions.q: If a gas is measured to be 980.5 torr (980.5 mmHg), what would the pressure be in atm? (Don't lose any sig figs!)
If a gas is measured to be 329 kPa, what would the pressure be in atm? (Don't lose any sig figs!)
FLASHBACK: If a gas is measured to be 302.1 mL, what would the volume be in L? (Don't lose any sig figs!)
Answer yes or no for each.

blanks.label: Does every gas calculation with a temperature variable require temperature be given or converted to Kelvin?
Combined gas law: do the pressure units both have to be in atm?
Combined gas law: do the volume units both have to be in liters?

questions.note: Temperature must ALWAYS be in Kelvin. In the combined gas law P and V just have to match each other (both mmHg, both mL, etc.).

questions.q: A 12.4 L cylinder contains a sample of gas at 2.54 atm. What pressure would the gas be in a 10.6 L cylinder at this same temperature?
questions.note: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ → P₂ = (2.54 × 12.4) ÷ 10.6 = 2.97 atm. Smaller volume → higher pressure.

questions.q: A 13.3 L cylinder contains a sample of gas at 14.5 atm. What pressure would the gas be in a 7.3 L cylinder at this same temperature? Report your answer in atmospheres to the ones position.
A gas with a pressure of 435 mmHg and a volume of 25.1 mL has a pressure change to 401.1 mmHg at constant temperature. What is the new volume of the gas?
questions.note: V₂ = (435 × 25.1) ÷ 401.1 = 27.2 mL. Units don't need converting because both pressures are mmHg.

questions.q: A gas volume is 64.91 L at 8.747 atm. The pressure of the gas changed to 1.409 atm at the same temperature. What is the final volume of the gas?
questions.given: For full credit: correct sig figs and the unit.

questions.q: A gas with a temperature of 28 ºC and a volume of 23.5 mL is contracted to 14.6 mL at constant pressure. What is the new temperature of the gas?
questions.note: Charles's law in KELVIN: T₂ = 301.15 K × (14.6 ÷ 23.5) = 187.1 K → 187.1 − 273.15 = −86 °C. (187 is the trap: that's Kelvin, not °C.)

questions.q: A sample of gas initially at 160.0 mmHg and occupying 25.0 mL at 307.15 K is cooled to 299.15 K and expanded to 160.0 mL. What is the final pressure of the sample of gas?
A sample of gas initially at 160.0 mmHg and occupying 25.0 mL at 34 °C is cooled to 26.0 °C and expanded to 160.0 mL. What is the final pressure of the sample of gas?
questions.note: Same problem as the one before with °C: 34 + 273.15 = 307.15 K and 26.0 + 273.15 = 299.15 K → 24.3 mmHg.

questions.q: A 43.17 mL container holds gas initially at 11.65 °C and 253.7 torr. If the volume changes to 57.07 mL and the temperature changes to 26.3 °C, what is the final pressure of this gas in torr? Don't round early! Report your answer to four significant figures.
A sample of gas initially occupies 238 mL at 126 °C and 946 mmHg. What is the volume if the gas is cooled to 94 °C and the pressure is decreased to 547 mmHg?

A sample of gas in a 28.5 L container is initially at 15 °C and 701 mmHg. If the pressure is reduced to 479 mmHg and the temperature is increased to 75 °C, what is the final volume? Add 273 to convert to Kelvin. Report your answer in liters to three significant figures.
A sample of gas occupies 459 mL at 44.5 °C and 658 torr. What is the temperature if the gas is compressed to 250 mL and the pressure is changed to 759 torr?
If a mixture with equal moles of helium gas and neon gas is allowed to escape through a pinhole in a container, the escaping gas would contain more neon than helium.
questions.note: False. Lighter gases effuse faster (Graham's law), so the escaping gas has MORE helium (4.00 g/mol) than neon (20.18 g/mol).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true about helium gas and argon gas samples at the same temperature and pressure?
opts: 4.00 grams of helium will occupy the same volume as 39.95 grams of argon.
The same number of moles of each will occupy the same volume.
If you have twice as many moles of argon as helium, the volume of argon will be twice as large.
The same number of grams of each will occupy the same volume.
One mole each of helium and argon in a container will take up twice the volume of 1 mole of helium by itself.
questions.note: Avogadro's law: volume depends on MOLES, not grams. 4.00 g He and 39.95 g Ar are each 1 mole, so those match; equal grams are different mole amounts.
